text_blocks.snippet: In a heart attack, specific enzymes and proteins, collectively known as cardiac enzymes or biomarkers, are released into the bloodstream when heart muscle tissue is damaged. Measuring these levels in blood tests helps doctors diagnose heart attacks and assess the extent of damage. Troponin is the most commonly used and sensitive biomarker for detecting heart attacks.
snippet_highlighted_words: Troponin is the most commonly used and sensitive biomarker for detecting heart attacks

list.title: Troponin:
list.snippet: This protein is highly specific to heart muscle and is the preferred biomarker for diagnosing heart attacks. Troponin levels rise within hours of heart damage and remain elevated for several days, allowing for detection even in cases where the heart attack occurred earlier.

list.title: Creatine Kinase (CK):
list.snippet: This enzyme is also found in skeletal muscle and can be elevated after a heart attack, but it is not as specific to the heart as troponin.

list.title: CK-MB:
list.snippet: This is a subtype of CK that is more specific to the heart than total CK. It rises within hours of a heart attack but returns to normal within a couple of days, making it less useful for detecting heart attacks that occurred earlier.
